texto:
X made its Lead Gen Ads generally available to every advertiser worldwide on October 30, 2026, extending the in-feed form format to small and medium-sized businesses and to advertisers who buy through X Ads Manager on their own. A user taps the ad, completes a short form that never leaves X and submits contact details that the advertiser can export or send to its own systems. The format returned to X in August, almost a decade after Twitter announced the retirement of a near-identical product, and the general release arrived with a single customer case study that gives two different figures for how far that customer's cost per lead fell.
In Short
X, the social network that used to be called Twitter, now lets any business run ads with a small sign-up form that people fill in without leaving the app. Businesses use these forms to collect names and contact details from people who might buy from them, and X says this now includes small companies that set up their ads themselves. X says one early tester got leads far more cheaply, but the same announcement gives two different numbers for how much cheaper, so how well the format works for everyone else is still an open question.
What X switched on
The announcement appeared as a long-form Article on the @XBusiness account, titled "Lead Gen Ads Are Now Available to All Advertisers on X." Its opening sentence sets the scope. "Lead Gen ads are now generally available to all advertisers globally, including small and medium-sized businesses and self-serve advertisers, with the product live in X Ads Manager," according to X.
X calls the format "one of the most requested products from advertisers." The mechanics are those of lead ads on other platforms. A user taps the ad, "fills in a short form that stays on X, and submits it without being sent to an external page," according to the post. There is no landing page and no redirect. Once someone has completed one form, later forms "can be pre-filled, removing the usual friction of redirects and retyping." X frames the purpose in terms of timing: "The goal is to turn attention that is already happening on X into a usable lead while the moment is still active."
The post does not say which fields are pre-filled, where that data comes from, or whether users see the pre-filled values before submitting. Twitter's 2013 version of the product, discussed below, pre-filled a user's name, username and email address.
Formats, objective and the Leads Center
Four creative types support the forms: image, video, carousel and Timeline Takeover. Advertisers get "a dedicated Leads objective in Ads Manager and a Leads Center where submissions can be exported or passed to a CRM," according to X.
That second piece matters operationally. A lead captured inside a social platform is only useful once it reaches the sales or marketing team that has to call it, and the hand-off to a CRM is where many in-platform form programmes either work or stall. X does not name any CRM partners, describe an API connection or say whether leads can be pushed in real time rather than downloaded in batches. Nor does the post say how long submissions are kept in the Leads Center.
X lists the common uses as "booking demos or appointments, growing lists and waitlists, collecting quote requests, and driving registrations for events or webinars."
A second change: forms in the viewer's language
A shorter note at the end of the post describes a separate update that is also live. Form fields "now appear in the local language of the viewer, or whatever language is set as the browser preference," according to X.
For an advertiser running a single campaign across several markets, this means a form built once is displayed in the language of whoever sees it, rather than in the language the advertiser wrote it in. The post does not say whether the change applies only to standard field labels or also to questions the advertiser writes, and it lists no supported languages.
The executive quote
Monique Pintarelli, X's head of global advertising, is quoted in the post. "Advertisers have been asking for a simpler way to capture leads where the conversation is already happening," she said. "Lead Gen Ads deliver that, and making them available to everyone means more businesses, including smaller ones, can turn real-time attention into results across the full funnel."
The post gives her employer as "SpaceXSI." That appears to be a misspelling of SpaceXAI, the company name under which X's August press release for its Ads MCP server identified her. According to Social Media Today, SpaceX began operating under the SpaceXAI name in July 2026 after absorbing xAI in February, and X is now a division of the combined company.
One advertiser, two numbers
The evidence X offers is a single case study. micro1, which X describes as "a company hyperscaling in the data management space," needed to reach "a narrow audience of decision-makers at established companies." According to the post, "Every month without qualified leads meant fewer deals in the pipeline."
micro1 was "one of the first advertisers in the Lead Generation beta," according to X. It ran native Lead Gen Ads with "every lead sent straight to their CRM," and its team "layered lookalikes, keywords and executive titles so the ads reached the people who actually control their company's data."
X then lists four results:
- "5x average ROAS in Q3 2026"
- "75% lower cost-per-lead after switching to the Lead Generation objective"
- "acquisitions delivered within the first two weeks"
- "The CPL improvement allowed for 4.5x increased investment, with room to grow further"
A few lines later, the post quotes Daniel Warner, micro1's chief marketing officer. "Our core audience lives on X, so X Ads has been a natural fit since the early days of micro1," he said. "We recently cut our cost-per-lead for our acquisition program by 33%, with help from a team that's been amazing to work with since the beginning." He added that micro1 is "stoked to experiment more with the newly launched lead gen forms, AI optimizations, and targeting tools."
So which is it: 75% or 33%? The post does not reconcile the two. They may measure different things. X's figure is tied to the switch to the Lead Generation objective, while Warner's describes the acquisition programme as a whole, credits "a team" rather than the format, and is followed by a statement that micro1 still intends to experiment more with the lead gen forms. Read literally, Warner's wording leaves open whether his 33% has much to do with the forms at all.
The gap is not small. By PPC Land's calculation, a 75% cut means each lead costs a quarter of what it did, so the same budget buys four times as many leads. A 33% cut means the same budget buys about 1.5 times as many.
The other figures carry their own ambiguities. ROAS is an unusual headline measure for a lead generation programme, because a lead has no revenue attached until it converts, sometimes months later. X does not say what revenue the 5x figure counts, how it was attributed to X or over what window. "Acquisitions" is not defined: it could mean customers, deals or contracts. The "4.5x increased investment" has no baseline. X discloses no spend, no lead volume, no absolute cost per lead and no comparison period, which also rules out setting micro1's results against outside benchmarks such as WordStream's average search cost per lead of $66.69. And the advertiser was chosen by X.
From teaser to general availability
The rollout took roughly three months. X's business account posted a teaser on July 21, 2026 reading "Tap. Lead. Done. Coming soon to X Ads," which AdTechRadar embedded in its own report.
By late August the format was live. Social Media Today reported on August 26 that X had announced an updated lead gen ad with a coloured call-to-action bar on the promoted post, a native form opened with one tap, pre-filled later submissions and support for image, video, carousel and Timeline Takeover creatives. X claimed at the time that the format would produce more leads, higher lead quality and lower cost per lead, according to that report. MediaNews4U reported on August 28 that X described the ads as available to advertisers globally, with the Leads objective and the Leads Center already in place, and quoted Pintarelli under the SpaceXAI name.
That raises a question the October post does not answer. If the product was already described as globally available in August, what changed on October 30? X's new post calls the earlier phase a beta and adds two groups to the scope: small and medium-sized businesses and self-serve advertisers. It does not say whether those accounts were excluded before, whether the August availability ran only through managed sales, or which markets, if any, were held back. One use case has also dropped off the list. Sweepstakes appeared among the suggested uses in August, according to both outlets, but not in October. X gives no reason.
AdTechRadar's October 30 report, which says X "announced today that its Lead Gen Ads product is now available to all advertisers globally, including SMBs and self-serve buyers," refers to the product as "first teased over the summer" and does not mention the August release.
Twitter did this before
The format is not new to the company. Twitter debuted Lead Generation Cards in May 2013, according to Vator. The cards pre-filled a user's name, Twitter username and email address, so that a single click sent those details to the business. Twitter tested them with New Relic, Full Sail and Priceline and first offered them to managed clients.
On August 29, 2013, the cards became available to all advertisers, according to MarTech. The release added CSV download or CRM import, built-in analytics for spend, leads and cost per lead, and support for every language Twitter Ads supported at the time.
Three years later, Twitter withdrew them. Social Media Today reported on December 9, 2016 that Twitter had announced the removal of lead generation campaigns and cards as an advertising option, with creation ending in February and viewing ending in March. Clix Marketing reported on December 12, 2016 that Twitter had confirmed the deprecation in a community forum post, with lead gen creation through the API ending on February 1 and viewing through the API ending on March 1.
The parallels with 2026 are close. Then as now, the product moved from a limited group to all advertisers within about three months, the hand-off to a CRM was a selling point, and language support was part of the pitch. Social Media Today described X's August 2026 version as close to a replica of the format Twitter retired. Neither X's October post nor AdTechRadar's report mentions the earlier product or the reasons it was withdrawn.
Where X's ad business stands
The Leads objective fills a gap that was visible six months ago. When X announced on April 30, 2026 that it had rebuilt its entire ad platform from scratch, a commenter asked whether X had considered adding lead forms similar to Meta's lead generation ad units. X did not respond publicly. In August, the X Ads MCP server gave AI agents write access to live campaigns through 23 tools, and the only objective its documentation named was website clicks.
The announcement fits a sequence of products aimed at advertisers who measure results rather than reach. X rolled out a redesigned AI-powered ad platform for small and medium-sized businesses in October 2024, initially as a limited release, with AI audience targeting, automatic pixel creation and bid optimisation against a target return. In June 2026, X added Google Tag Manager integration and live diagnostics for its Pixel and Conversions API, a no-code route that matters most to smaller advertisers without developers. In July, Mentions Boost let Premium Business accounts pay to promote organic posts that mention them.
AdTechRadar reads the October release the same way. "X is putting more emphasis on driving results, while making its ad tools more accessible to smaller businesses," according to the publication. "This has always been the most sensible strategy, especially as larger advertisers pulled back due to brand safety concerns." AdTechRadar ties the rollout to earlier AI targeting and campaign tools aimed at small businesses, Grok-powered features to help smaller advertisers create ads and analyse campaigns, and the Ads Manager rebuild.
The backdrop is a smaller business than Twitter once was. X's ad revenues fell from $2.43 billion in 2021 to an estimated $1.25 billion in 2025, according to eMarketer, a decline that framed X's brand suitability playbook positioning Grok as a pre-bid scoring tool in March. Programmatic inventory on X has averaged CPMs of $0.39, against $6 to $8 for Meta, according to data from December 2024. Pintarelli has said, at CES, that 97 of the top 100 advertisers had returned to the platform. Regulatory pressure has not eased: the European Commission fined X EUR 120 million under the Digital Services Act on December 5, 2025 and opened a formal investigation into Grok on January 26, 2026.
AdTechRadar's verdict is cautious. "For all the controversy surrounding the platform, its ads business seems to have a clearer product focus than it has in recent years," its editors wrote. "The question now is whether these improvements actually deliver results for advertisers. X says they do, but given the platform's past controversies, it will need to keep proving its value."
A crowded format
X arrives in a mature category. LinkedIn's Lead Gen Forms are the reference point for business-to-business advertisers, and in April 2026 LinkedIn extended them to Event Ads with a lead gen objective and routing into CRM or marketing automation systems. On October 29, 2026, Reddit said its Max campaigns now support lead gen objectives, with leads routed into CRM workflows and HubSpot being tested as a platform partner. Google gave advertisers a native Leads screen in June that holds form leads for no more than 60 days. Quora launched lead gen form ads in January 2020, with twelve standard fields and automatic CRM delivery.
What X brings is the claim in Pintarelli's quote: real-time attention, captured while a conversation is happening. Whether that attention converts into qualified leads at lower cost than LinkedIn, Meta or Reddit is what the micro1 case study is meant to show, and what its inconsistent figures leave unsettled.
Lead quality is the other test. A Lunio analysis of 64 million clicks found that LinkedIn drew the most bot clicks per ad dollar, with an average invalid traffic rate of 15.34%, and said bots exploit Lead Gen Forms to flood advertiser CRMs with junk leads. Google stated in September that its filters do not prevent invalid leads on their own and pointed advertisers to reCAPTCHA, double opt-in and server-side validation. X's post says nothing about invalid lead detection, spam controls on forms or credits for fraudulent submissions.
What the post leaves out
Several things an advertiser would need before committing budget are absent from X's announcement:
- Bidding and pricing. The post introduces a Leads objective but does not say what it optimises for, whether bids can be set on a cost-per-lead basis or how leads are charged.
- Form contents. There is no list of available fields, no mention of custom questions and no description of which data is pre-filled.
- Data handling. X does not say how long the Leads Center keeps submissions, what users are told about where their details go or how the advertiser's own privacy policy is shown.
- Integrations. "Passed to a CRM" is the only description of the connection. No CRM is named, and the post does not say whether the Leads objective is available through the Ads API or the Ads MCP server.
- Scope. "All advertisers globally" is the only geographic statement. Any excluded markets or restricted categories go unmentioned.
Why this matters for marketers
For business-to-business marketers whose buyers are active on X, the release removes the landing page from the path between an ad and a sales conversation, and it does so inside a self-serve tool that small businesses can use without a sales contract. That is the main practical change. It also gives X a performance objective it lacked when it relaunched Ads Manager in April, and closes a product gap that has existed since Twitter withdrew its lead generation cards in early 2017.
The evidence for the format's results is limited. X has published one case study, picked by X, from one advertiser, with figures that do not agree with each other and no absolute numbers. AdTechRadar's caution, that X "will need to keep proving its value," sits alongside a revenue line that has roughly halved since 2021 and a regulator in Brussels still examining Grok. Advertisers who already run lead forms on LinkedIn, Meta, Google or Reddit now have one more platform to compare, with almost no public data to compare it on.

Summary
Who: X, the social network that is now a division of SpaceXAI, and its head of global advertising, Monique Pintarelli. The case study features micro1 and its chief marketing officer, Daniel Warner. AdTechRadar reported on the release.
What: X made Lead Gen Ads generally available to all advertisers globally, including small and medium-sized businesses and self-serve advertisers. The format puts a short, pre-fillable form inside image, video, carousel and Timeline Takeover ads, with a dedicated Leads objective and a Leads Center for export or CRM hand-off. A separate update displays form fields in the viewer's language. X's case study reports a 75% lower cost per lead for micro1, while micro1's CMO cites a 33% cut.
When: October 30, 2026, following a July 21 teaser and an initial release in late August 2026. Twitter had offered a similar product from 2013 until announcing its removal in December 2016.
Where: Globally, in X Ads Manager.
Why: X is building out performance advertising tools and courting smaller advertisers as its ad revenue has fallen from $2.43 billion in 2021 to an estimated $1.25 billion in 2025, according to eMarketer. The release gives X a lead generation objective that LinkedIn, Google, Reddit and others already offer, though the only public evidence of its results is a single case study with conflicting figures.
